title: Ali Fazal Puts On a Uniform and Walks Into 1978 Delhi. Raakh Might Be the Darkest Thing You Stream This Year.
excerpt: Based on one of India's most horrifying real-life criminal cases, this Paatal Lok director's new 8-part thriller arrives Thursday on Prime Video with Sonali Bendre in her most intense role yet.
body:
There are comfortable watches and there are necessary ones, and then there is **Raakh**, which lands on **Amazon Prime Video** this Thursday, June 12, looking like it plans to crawl under your skin and stay there.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=RdB_TgwLPqs</youtube>

The eight-episode series is set in 1978 Delhi — before CCTV, before social media, before a missing child's photo could reach a million phones in minutes. When two teenagers vanish without a trace, the city doesn't scroll past the news. It sits with it. And **Sub-Inspector Jayprakash**, played by **Ali Fazal** in his first-ever cop role, is the man tasked with finding them before the trail goes cold.

Directed by **Prosit Roy** — the man who gave us the most unforgettable episodes of *Paatal Lok* Season 1 — *Raakh* draws its bones from the real-life **Ranga-Billa case**, one of the most infamous kidnapping and murder cases in Indian criminal history. The 1978 abduction of **Geeta and Sanjay Chopra** in Delhi led to a nationwide manhunt that gripped the country for weeks and ultimately resulted in two of India's most notorious criminal executions. The case changed how India talked about child safety. It changed laws. It changed Delhi.

*Raakh* fictionalizes the investigation, but the dread is real.

> "I have never played a cop before this. It's a very interesting timeline to be a part of. It feels fresh and relatively new." — **Ali Fazal**

Fazal — who has spent the last few years moving between Hollywood (*Death on the Nile*, the *Mirzapur* saga) and international festivals — is a compelling choice for the role. He's never carried a badge on screen, and there's something magnetic about watching an actor known for charisma and vulnerability navigate the blunt-instrument world of '70s Indian policing. His wife **Richa Chadha** saw the first-look poster and left a single comment: *"Woof! Keep that uniform."* The internet agreed.


Then there is **Sonali Bendre**, who continues what has quietly become one of Bollywood's most impressive comeback arcs. After her acclaimed turn in *The Broken News*, Bendre could have returned to the comfort of legacy stardom — magazine covers, reality show panels, the safe nostalgia circuit. Instead, she chose this: a raw, emotionally layered role in a series about the worst things people do to each other. When the writers narrated the story, she said something that tells you exactly where she is in her career.

> "Even if I had to just stand in the background, I would have said yes." — **Sonali Bendre**

**Aamir Bashir**, **Dibyendu Bhattacharya**, and **Rakesh Bedi** round out a cast that reads like a carefully assembled ensemble rather than a star vehicle. Created and written by **Anusha Nandakumar** and **Sandeep Saket**, with dialogues by **Ayush Trivedi**, the series promises the kind of slow-burn tension that Indian crime television has been building toward but rarely delivers at this level.

Prosit Roy has described *Raakh* as "a deeply immersive world that pushes boundaries while exploring the complex layers of human nature." Coming from the director who made the Chitrakoot episodes of *Paatal Lok* feel like descending into a specific circle of hell, that's not a throwaway line. That's a promise.

**Prime Video India's head of originals Nikhil Madhok** called it "one of the most powerful stories we have told on Prime Video." Given that Prime Video's Indian originals slate includes *Mirzapur*, *Paatal Lok*, *The Family Man*, and *Panchayat*, that's a claim worth paying attention to.

For the diaspora, the access story is simple: *Raakh* premieres globally on **Prime Video in over 240 countries and territories** — no VPN juggling, no geo-restrictions, no weeks-long delay. If you have a Prime subscription in New York, Toronto, London, or Sydney, you get *Raakh* the same Thursday as someone in Delhi.

It arrives alongside a stacked OTT day — **Bhooth Bangla** on Netflix and **Karuppu** on Prime Video both drop June 12 — making it arguably the biggest single streaming day of 2026 for Indian content. But while Bhooth Bangla brings Priyadarshan's crowd-pleasing horror-comedy and Karuppu delivers Suriya's blockbuster action, *Raakh* is the one that will keep you up past 2 AM. Not because it's fun. Because you won't be able to stop.

The 1978 case that inspired it haunted a generation. The series arriving this Thursday is built to haunt another.

Eight episodes. All dropping at once. Clear your Thursday night.
